newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Moslems sentenced in "farce" trial in Serb court.
newsitem.headline: Moslems sentenced in "farce" trial in Serb court.

text.p: A Bosnian Serb court jailed seven Bosnian Moslems on Thursday after a murder trial which the international community had labelled a "travesty", "farce" and "fundamentally flawed".

Despite heavy international criticism and pressure, the court in Zvornik handed down 20-year prison terms on three Moslem men accused of murdering four Serbs and sentenced the other four to one year each for illegal possession of firearms.
The United Nations mission in Bosnia quickly condemned the proceedings and urged the authorities of the Bosnian Serb Republika Srpska to hold a retrial in keeping with international norms.
"The United Nations condemns the proceedings in a Republika Srpska court which led to the conviction of three defendants in the Zvornik Seven trial.

"These proceedings must be characterized as fundamentally flawed and the U.N. mission calls on (Bosnian Serb) judicial authorities to order a prompt retrial of the three persons convicted...in accordance with the standards contained in the European Convention on Human Rights," it said in a statement.

The Serb court denied the Moslem defendants the right to be represented by lawyers from the Moslem-Croat federation and appointed Serb attorneys who were given just five minutes to present their defence.
But the court stopped short of passing the death penalties the prosecution had requested.
"(The Bosnian Serb republic) is one of the signatories of the Dayton agreement and, under Dayton documents, the death penalty is not allowed," presiding judge Petar Stjepanovic said.
The group of seven Moslems claimed to be survivors of wartime massacres in the Moslem enclave of Srebrenica.
They said they had hidden in caves and forests since the enclave fell to Serbs in July 1995.
The men, first spotted by U.S. NATO troops while moving on foot in the forest, surrendered to U.S. soldiers voluntarily.

They were questioned and handed over to the Serb police because they were found in possession of some grenades and pistols, making them technically an armed group in violation of the Dayton peace agreement.

But subsequent reports indicated the Moslems should have been kept in U.S. army custody until it could be established whether, as survivors of the Serb conquest of Srebrenica, they had violated the accord.
The trial failed to produce conclusive evidence to prove the defendants were guilty of the crimes they were charged with, a U.N. spokesman said.
"To our knowledge there was no connection established between the defendants and the crime during the court's proceedings on Tuesday," Alex Ivanko said.

A spokesman for the international High Representative to Bosnia, Carl Bildt, said efforts to put pressure on Serb authorities, already widely condemned for their poor human rights record, would continue.
Speaking before the court's ruling, spokesman Michael Maclay said: "Irrespective of what the verdict is today the international community is not going to let whatever emerges go uncontested."
Maclay said further funding of reconstruction in the Bosnian Serb part of the country would be discussed, but declined to go into detail.

"All we can say at the moment is there will be a relationship between the way this trial is perceived and what they (Serbs) stand to gain from the international community's generosity in putting in funds," he said.
"We've made very clear to Republika Srpska authorities that there will be consequences from this trial."
The Bosnian Serbs received only two percent of $1.2 billion which foreign donors gave for Bosnian reconstruction in 1996 because of their defiance of the peace accord's civilian provisions.
